body: The position vector of a point is denoted \vec{r}, and the unit vector in the direction of the position vector is denoted \hat{r}.
title: Position vector and its unit vector

body: \vec{C} = \vec{A} + \vec{B} = (A_x + B_x)\hat{i} + (A_y + B_y)\hat{j}
title: Resultant vector (sum of components)

body: A scalar is a quantity described by magnitude only.
title: Scalar quantity

body: The CED's examples of scalar and vector quantities in kinematics.

items.label: Scalar: distance
items.meaning: Magnitude only

items.label: Scalar: speed
items.meaning: Magnitude only

items.label: Vector: position
items.meaning: Magnitude and direction

items.label: Vector: displacement
items.meaning: Magnitude and direction

items.label: Vector: velocity
items.meaning: Magnitude and direction

items.label: Vector: acceleration
items.meaning: Magnitude and direction

title: Scalar vs. vector examples

body: In a given one-dimensional coordinate system, opposite directions are denoted by opposite signs.
title: Signs in one dimension

body: \vec{r} = A\hat{i} + B\hat{j} + C\hat{k}
title: Unit vector notation

body: A vector is drawn as an arrow whose direction is the vector's direction and whose length is proportional to its magnitude.

items.label: Arrow direction
items.meaning: Direction of the vector

items.label: Arrow length
items.meaning: Proportional to the vector's magnitude

title: Vector arrow representation

body: A vector is a quantity described by both magnitude and direction.
title: Vector quantity

body: \vec{a}_{avg} = \frac{\Delta \vec{v}}{\Delta t}
title: Average acceleration

body: \vec{v}_{avg} = \frac{\Delta \vec{r}}{\Delta t}
caution: The CED denotes position by the vector r (1.1.A.4.ii), so the displacement here is the change in the position vector. Along a single axis the component form, change in x over change in t, is used instead.
title: Average velocity

body: \Delta x = x - x_0
title: Displacement

body: \vec{a} = \frac{d\vec{v}}{dt}, \qquad a_x = \frac{dv_x}{dt}
title: Instantaneous acceleration

body: As the time interval used to calculate an average value of a quantity approaches zero, the average approaches the value of the quantity at that instant, called the instantaneous value.
title: Instantaneous value

body: \vec{v} = \frac{d\vec{r}}{dt}, \qquad v_x = \frac{dx}{dt}
title: Instantaneous velocity

body: Time-dependent position, velocity, and acceleration functions are related by differentiation (position to velocity to acceleration) and integration (the reverse).
title: Moving between x(t), v(t), and a(t)

body: In the object model the size, shape, and internal configuration are ignored, and the object may be treated as a single point with extensive properties such as mass and charge.
title: Object model

body: An object is accelerating if the magnitude and/or the direction of its velocity is changing.
caution: Acceleration is not only speeding up or negative values; slowing down and changing direction also count, and the sign depends on the chosen axis.
title: When an object is accelerating

body: \Delta v_x = \int_{t_1}^{t_2} a_x(t)\,dt
title: Change in velocity from area under a–t graph

body: x = x_0 + v_{x0} t + \tfrac{1}{2} a_x t^2
caution: Valid only for constant acceleration; written for x but usable in any single dimension.
title: Constant acceleration: position-time equation

caution: Valid only for constant acceleration; written for x but usable in any single dimension.
title: Constant acceleration: velocity-position equation

body: v_x = v_{x0} + a_x t
caution: Valid only for constant acceleration; written for x but usable in any single dimension.
title: Constant acceleration: velocity-time equation

body: \Delta x = \int_{t_1}^{t_2} v_x(t)\,dt
title: Displacement from area under v–t graph

body: Near Earth's surface the vertical acceleration due to gravity is downward and constant, with g \approx 10 m/s^2 used for numerical work.
caution: The 10 m/s^2 value is the expected one, but correctly using 9.8 or 9.81 m/s^2 is not penalized.
title: Gravitational acceleration near Earth

body: Relationships among position, velocity, and acceleration graphs as functions of time.

items.label: Slope of tangent on x–t graph
items.meaning: Instantaneous velocity, v_x = dx/dt

items.label: Slope of tangent on v–t graph
items.meaning: Instantaneous acceleration, a_x = dv_x/dt

items.label: Area under v–t curve
items.meaning: Displacement during the interval

items.label: Area under a–t curve
items.meaning: Change in velocity during the interval

title: Reading x(t), v(t), a(t) graphs

body: The CED's five ways to represent motion.

items.label: Motion diagrams
items.meaning: Representation of motion

items.label: Figures
items.meaning: Representation of motion

items.label: Graphs
items.meaning: Representation of motion

items.label: Equations
items.meaning: Representation of motion

items.label: Narrative descriptions
items.meaning: Representation of motion

title: Representations of motion

body: The acceleration of any object is the same as measured from all inertial reference frames.
title: Acceleration is the same in all inertial frames

body: Unless otherwise stated, the frame of reference of any problem may be assumed to be inertial.
title: Default frame assumption

body: The choice of reference frame determines the direction and magnitude of quantities measured by an observer in that frame.
title: Reference frame determines measurements

body: The observed velocity of an object combines the object's velocity and the velocity of the observer's reference frame, using vector addition or subtraction to convert between frames.
title: Relative velocity by vector addition

body: Motion in two dimensions is analyzed with one-dimensional kinematic relationships applied to each component separately, and motion in one dimension can change without changing a perpendicular dimension.
title: Analyze 2D motion by components

body: Velocity and acceleration may be different in each dimension and may be nonuniform.
title: Components may differ and be nonuniform

body: Projectile motion is a special case of two-dimensional motion with zero acceleration in one dimension and constant, nonzero acceleration in the second dimension.
title: Projectile motion

body: \vec{r}_{cm}=\frac{\int \vec{r}\,dm}{\int dm}
title: Center of mass of a continuous object

body: x_{cm}=\frac{\sum_i m_i x_i}{\sum_i m_i}
title: Center of mass of discrete masses

body: For objects or systems with symmetrical mass distributions, the center of mass lies on lines of symmetry, and a system can be modeled as a single object located at its center of mass.
title: Center of mass of symmetric objects

body: \lambda=\frac{dm}{d\ell}
title: Linear mass density

body: If the properties or interactions of the constituent objects are not important to the behavior being modeled, the system can itself be treated as a single object.
title: System treated as a single object

body: M_{total}=\int \rho\,dV
caution: Integrate over length, area, or volume depending on whether the density is given in one, two, or three dimensions.
title: Total mass from a density function

body: A contact force describes the interaction of an object or system touching another and is a macroscopic effect of interatomic electric forces.
title: Contact force

body: A force is a vector quantity describing an interaction between two objects or systems; an object or system cannot exert a net force on itself.
title: Force

body: A diagram of a single object or system showing every force exerted on it by the environment.
caution: On the AP exam draw individual forces only, not force components, on the free-body diagram.

items.label: Dot
items.meaning: Represents the center of mass; all force vectors originate here

items.label: Force arrows
items.meaning: Each force exerted by the environment is drawn as its own straight arrow pointing in the direction of the force

items.label: Same-direction forces
items.meaning: Drawn side by side, not overlapping

items.label: Coordinate axis
items.meaning: One axis chosen parallel to the direction of acceleration (e.g., along an incline)

title: Free-body diagram

body: Model assumptions for strings and pulleys, with the contrast for a massive string.

items.label: Ideal string
items.meaning: Negligible mass and does not stretch under tension

items.label: Tension in ideal string
items.meaning: Same at all points within the string

items.label: String with nonnegligible mass
items.meaning: Tension may not be the same at all points

items.label: Ideal pulley
items.meaning: Negligible mass; rotates about an axle through its center of mass with negligible friction

title: Ideal string and ideal pulley

body: Interactions between objects within a system (internal forces) do not influence the motion of the system's center of mass.
title: Internal forces and the center of mass

body: \vec{F}_{A\ on\ B}=-\vec{F}_{B\ on\ A}
caution: The paired forces act on different objects, so they never cancel in a single object's free-body diagram.
title: Newton's third law

body: Tension is the macroscopic net result of the forces that infinitesimal segments of a string, cable, chain, or similar system exert on each other in response to an external force.
caution: Tension is uniform only for an ideal string (negligible mass, does not stretch). In a string with nonnegligible mass, tension may differ from point to point.
title: Tension

body: Forces may be balanced in one dimension and unbalanced in another, and the velocity changes only in the direction of the unbalanced force.
title: Balanced in one dimension, unbalanced in another

body: An inertial reference frame is one from which an observer would verify Newton's first law of motion.
title: Inertial reference frame

body: \vec{F}_{net}=\sum_i \vec{F}_i = 0
caution: Net force is the vector sum of all forces exerted on the system. Translational equilibrium is the case where that sum is zero, so velocity stays constant. Forces can balance in one dimension and not in another, and velocity changes only along the unbalanced direction.
title: Net force and translational equilibrium

body: If the net force exerted on a system is zero, the velocity of that system remains constant.
title: Newton's first law

body: \vec{a}_{sys}=\frac{\sum\vec{F}}{m_{sys}}=\frac{\vec{F}_{net}}{m_{sys}}
caution: The acceleration is that of the system's center of mass, and it points in the direction of the net force.
title: Newton's second law

body: The velocity of a system's center of mass changes only if a nonzero net external force is exerted on the system.
title: When the center-of-mass velocity changes

body: The magnitude of a system's apparent weight is the magnitude of the normal force exerted on it, which differs from the gravitational force when the system accelerates.
caution: Apparent weight is the normal force, not the gravitational force.
title: Apparent weight

body: An observer in a noninertial reference frame cannot distinguish between an object's apparent weight and the gravitational force exerted on it by a gravitational field.
title: Equivalence principle

body: |\vec{g}|=\frac{|\vec{F}_g|}{m}=\frac{GM}{r^2}
caution: M is the mass of the system creating the field and m is the test object. When gravity is the only force on an object, its acceleration in m/s^2 is numerically equal to g in N/kg at that location.
title: Gravitational field strength

body: Inertial mass (inertia) determines how much an object's motion resists change when interacting with another object; gravitational mass is related to the attractive force between two systems with mass; the two are experimentally verified to be equivalent.
title: Inertial mass vs. gravitational mass

body: F_g=\frac{G m_1 m_2}{r^2}
caution: r is the distance between the systems' centers of mass; the force is attractive and acts along the line connecting the centers of mass.
title: Newton's law of universal gravitation

body: Net gravitational force from a uniform spherical shell or sphere on an object, depending on location (the theorem need not be proved).
caution: Do not prove or derive the shell theorem; state and apply the results.

items.label: Inside a thin spherical shell
items.meaning: Net gravitational force is zero

items.label: Outside a thin spherical shell
items.meaning: Treat the shell as a single mass at its center

items.label: Inside a uniform sphere
items.meaning: Only the partial mass at distance less than or equal to the object's distance from the center contributes

title: Newton's shell theorem results

body: m_{partial}=\rho\,\tfrac{4}{3}\pi r_{partial}^3,\qquad F_{g,partial}=-k\,r_{partial}
title: Partial mass and force inside a uniform sphere

body: \text{Weight}=F_g=mg
caution: Near Earth's surface g is about 10 N/kg; when gravity is the only force, the acceleration in m/s^2 equals the field strength in N/kg.
title: Weight

body: A system appears weightless when no forces are exerted on it or when the force of gravity is the only force exerted on it.
title: When a system appears weightless

body: If the gravitational force between two systems' centers of mass changes negligibly as their relative position changes, it can be treated as constant between the initial and final positions.
title: When gravitational force is constant

body: Kinetic friction opposes each surface's motion relative to the other, and does not depend on the contact surface area; the coefficient depends on the surface materials.
title: Direction and dependence of kinetic friction

body: F_{f,k}=\mu_k F_N
title: Kinetic friction magnitude

body: The normal force is the perpendicular component of the force a surface exerts on an object in contact with it, directed away from the surface.
title: Normal force

body: F_{f,s}\le \mu_s F_N,\qquad F_{f,s,max}=\mu_s F_N
caution: Static friction is an inequality that takes whatever value and direction prevents slipping; use the equality only at the slipping threshold.
title: Static friction (inequality and maximum)

body: The coefficient of static friction is typically greater than the coefficient of kinetic friction for a given pair of surfaces.
caution: The CED says "typically," not always.
title: Static versus kinetic coefficient

body: \vec{F}_s=-k\,\Delta\vec{x}
caution: Δx is measured from the spring's relaxed length; the force is directed toward the equilibrium position of the object-spring system.
title: Hooke's law

body: An ideal spring has negligible mass and exerts a force proportional to the change in its length from its relaxed length; a nonideal spring has nonnegligible mass or a force not proportional to that change.
title: Ideal spring

body: k_{eq}=\sum_i k_i=k_1+k_2+\cdots
title: Springs in parallel

body: \frac{1}{k_{eq}}=\sum_i\frac{1}{k_i}=\frac{1}{k_1}+\frac{1}{k_2}+\cdots
caution: k_eq in series is smaller than the smallest individual spring constant. Only pure series or pure parallel combinations are expected, not mixed.
title: Springs in series

body: \vec{F}_r=-k\vec{v}
caution: A resistive force is velocity-dependent and opposite the object's velocity.
title: Resistive force

body: Steps for finding velocity, position, and acceleration of an object under a resistive force such as F_r = -kv.

items.meaning: Apply Newton's second law to the object with the resistive force, which gives a differential equation for velocity.
Use separation of variables to solve for the velocity.
Integrate over the proper limits of integration.
With velocity known as a function of time, use initial conditions and calculus to get position or acceleration.
Check the result: for F_r = -kv, position, velocity, and acceleration are exponential in time, with asymptotes set by the initial conditions and the forces exerted.
For terminal velocity, the maximum speed under a constant force and an opposing resistive force, set the net force equal to zero.

title: Solving motion under a resistive force

body: Terminal velocity is the maximum speed achieved by an object under a constant force and an opposing resistive force, reached when the net force on the object is zero.
title: Terminal velocity

body: a_c=\frac{v^2}{r}
caution: Directed toward the center of the circular path; it can come from one force, several forces, or force components, not a separate extra force.
title: Centripetal acceleration

body: T^2=\frac{4\pi^2}{GM}R^3
caution: Kepler's first and second laws are not expected; the centripetal acceleration comes only from gravitational attraction by the central body.
title: Kepler's third law (circular orbit)

body: v=\sqrt{gr}
caution: Valid only at the top of the loop, where gravity alone supplies the centripetal acceleration.
title: Minimum speed at top of a vertical loop

body: T=\frac{1}{f},\qquad T=\frac{2\pi r}{v}
title: Period and frequency in uniform circular motion

body: In each named case, identify which force or force components supply the centripetal acceleration toward the center of the circular path.
caution: Centripetal force is not a separate force on a free-body diagram. Name the actual forces, or their components, that point toward the center.

items.label: Top of a vertical loop (minimum speed)
items.meaning: Gravity is the only force causing the centripetal acceleration, which gives v = \sqrt{gr}.

items.label: Banked surface
items.meaning: Components of the static friction force and the normal force contribute to the net force producing centripetal acceleration.

items.label: Conical pendulum
items.meaning: A component of the tension contributes to the net force producing centripetal acceleration.

items.label: Satellite in circular orbit
items.meaning: Gravitational attraction alone causes the centripetal acceleration.

title: Sources of centripetal force in named cases

body: Tangential acceleration is the rate at which speed changes and is tangent to the circular path; the net acceleration is the vector sum of the centripetal and tangential accelerations.
title: Tangential and net acceleration

body: AP Physics C: Mechanics only expects analysis of the transfer of mechanical energy, though mechanical energy may be dissipated as thermal energy or sound by nonconservative forces.
title: Boundary: mechanical energy only

body: Translational kinetic energy is a scalar, and different observers may measure different values of K for the same object depending on their frame of reference.
title: Kinetic energy is a scalar and depends on reference frame

body: K = \tfrac{1}{2} m v^{2}
title: Translational kinetic energy

body: E_{\text{mech}} = K + U
title: Mechanical energy

body: The work done by a conservative force is path-independent, depends only on the initial and final configurations, and is zero if the system returns to its initial configuration.
title: Conservative force work

body: \vec{A}\cdot\vec{B} = AB\cos\theta
title: Dot product magnitude

body: E_{\text{dissipated}}\approx F_{f}\,s,\quad s=\text{length of the path over which the force is exerted}
caution: The CED says this is typically equated to friction force times the length of the path, so use path length, not net displacement.
title: Energy dissipated by friction

body: The work done by a nonconservative force is path-dependent, and the most common nonconservative forces are friction and air resistance, whereas the work done by a conservative force depends only on the initial and final configurations and is zero if the system returns to its initial configuration.
title: Nonconservative force work

body: Only the component of the force parallel to the displacement of the point of application of the force changes the system's total energy. A component perpendicular to the direction of the displacement of the system's center of mass can change the direction of the system's motion without changing its kinetic energy.
title: Only the parallel force component changes the system's energy

body: Potential energies are associated only with conservative forces.
title: Potential energy only for conservative forces

body: Work is the amount of energy transferred into or out of a system by a force exerted on that system over a distance.
title: Work

body: Work equals the area under the curve of a graph of F∥ as a function of displacement.
title: Work as area under an F∥ vs. displacement graph

body: W=F_{\parallel}\,d=Fd\cos\theta
caution: This is a derived special case of the line integral, valid only when the parallel component of the force is constant; use the integral otherwise.
title: Work by a force with constant parallel component

body: W=\int_a^b \vec{F}\cdot d\vec{r}
title: Work done by a variable force (line integral)

body: Work is a scalar quantity that may be positive, negative, or zero.
title: Work is a scalar with sign

body: \Delta K=\sum_i W_i
caution: The sum is the net work done by all forces exerted on the object (3.2.A.4). For a variable force each W_i is the line integral of the force along the path (3.2.A.3); the force-times-displacement form applies only where that force's parallel component is constant (3.2.A.3.iii).
title: Work–energy theorem

body: U_{s} = \tfrac{1}{2} k (\Delta x)^{2}
caution: U_s is never negative; it does not change sign between stretched and compressed.
title: Elastic potential energy of an ideal spring

body: F_{x} = -\frac{dU(x)}{dx}
title: Force from potential energy

body: U_g=-G\frac{m_1m_2}{r}
title: General gravitational potential energy

body: \Delta U_g=mg\,\Delta y
caution: This is only an approximation valid near the surface where the gravitational field is nearly constant; use -Gm_1m_2/r for large changes in distance.
title: Gravitational potential energy near a planet's surface

body: \Delta U = -\int_{a}^{b} \vec{F}_{cf}\cdot d\vec{r}
title: Potential energy change from a conservative force

body: A system of two or more objects has potential energy if the objects interact only through conservative forces, and it is a scalar associated with the positions of objects in the system.
title: Potential energy of a system

body: U_{\text{total}}=\sum_{\text{pairs}}U_{ij}
title: Potential energy of multi-object systems

body: Stable equilibrium is a location at which a small displacement results in a force opposite to the displacement, accelerating the object back toward equilibrium; it occurs at a local minimum of U(x).
title: Stable equilibrium

body: Unstable equilibrium is a location at which a small displacement results in a force in the same direction as the displacement, accelerating the object away from equilibrium; it occurs at a local maximum of U(x).
title: Unstable equilibrium

body: The definition of zero potential energy for a system is a decision made by the observer to simplify or assist analysis.
title: Zero of potential energy is a choice

body: Students must know that mechanical energy can be dissipated as thermal energy or sound by nonconservative forces.
title: Boundary: dissipation by nonconservative forces

body: Any change to one type of energy in a system must be balanced by an equivalent change in other types within the system or by a transfer of energy between the system and its surroundings.
title: Energy balance within and across system boundaries

body: If the work done on the selected system is zero and there are no nonconservative interactions within it, total mechanical energy is constant; if the work is nonzero, energy is transferred between the system and the environment.
caution: Energy is conserved in all interactions; state the chosen system when claiming mechanical energy is or is not constant.
title: System choice determines whether energy changes

body: A system of a single object can only have kinetic energy, while a system with objects interacting via conservative forces or that can change shape reversibly may have both kinetic and potential energies.
title: Which systems can have which energies

body: P_{\text{avg}} = \frac{\Delta E}{\Delta t} = \frac{W}{\Delta t}
title: Average power

body: P_{\text{inst}} = \frac{dW}{dt}
title: Instantaneous power

body: P_{\text{inst}} = F_{\parallel} v = F v\cos\theta
title: Instantaneous power from a constant force

body: Power is the rate at which energy changes with respect to time, either by transfer into or out of a system or by conversion from one type to another within a system.
title: Power
